domain: multi-tenant trust-boundary enforcement, fail-closed constraint design, and phased-rollout security for multi-harness agentic systems
axioms: 'Fail closed' is an implementation obligation, not a design intent — it only holds if every code path capable of selecting a destination is provably required to consult the constraint before acting, with no alternate path (legacy shim, partially-migrated adapter) that can bypass it.

A phased rollout must uphold its safety guarantees at every intermediate state, not only at the final architecture — a constraint that is enforced end-to-end only once all phases ship is unenforced during the entire rollout window.

A label that gates a security-relevant decision (e.g. trust-zone/data-sensitivity) is only trustworthy if its origin and mutability are defined; an unlabeled or spoofable input defeats the constraint regardless of how correctly the constraint itself is written.

Emitting a control (e.g. a verification gate) is not the same as enforcing it; a router that outputs 'behavioral-verify required' has only shifted responsibility to the consumer, and that handoff must be independently verified, not assumed.

A compatibility shim built to preserve old call sites is, from a security standpoint, a hole through the new enforcement layer unless it is explicitly proven to route through the same constraint checks as the new path.

State that spans trust or harness boundaries (failure counters, escalation state, evidence provenance) must have an explicit scope; if the scope is undefined, the default behavior is fragmentation (state silently resets or forks) rather than continuity.
An evidence or telemetry store that accepts self-reported origin metadata without authentication is a tamperable input to any downstream automated system (e.g. a policy-proposal flow) that trusts it.
primitives: enforcement locus (where a constraint is actually checked vs. where a decision is merely emitted)
code path / call site that can reach a destination-selection decision
intermediate rollout state (a phase boundary where only some adapters/harnesses are migrated)
verification gate (a required check attached to a routing decision)
failure_mode: Reasons primarily about enforcement structure and bypass paths, so it tends to accept a capability or benchmark value (e.g. reward_hack_risk score) as given rather than questioning whether that value was validly measured — that validity question belongs to the benchmark-provenance lens.

Focuses on security/enforcement gaps and can under-weight pure schema-evolvability concerns (e.g. whether a registry key survives a rename) unless the rename also happens to create a security bypass — general schema hygiene issues without a security angle fall outside its natural pull.

Prioritizes intermediate-state and cross-harness bypass risk so heavily that it can miss single-harness, single-phase issues that are real but don't involve a boundary crossing — its lens is calibrated for the seams, not the interior of any one component.
